title: How to choose a web design agency for your business
seoTitle: How to Choose a Web Design Agency | ALYOXA Insights
description: A practical guide to choosing a web design agency: assess relevant work, process, technical quality, ownership, and the details behind a proposal.
primaryKeyword: how to choose a web design agency
supportingKeywords: web design agency for small businesses
excerpt: Look beyond the first impression. Find the team that understands what your website needs to do.
intro: Choose a web design agency by how well it connects your business goals with design, content, and development. A beautiful portfolio is a useful starting point, but a clear scope, a credible process, and a maintainable result matter just as much.
takeaway: Before comparing agencies, write down your audience, the action you want visitors to take, and the constraints the project must respect.

sections.title: Define the job before choosing the team
paragraphs: A first website for a new consultancy and a redesign for an established product business need different kinds of support. Describe what has changed, who the site must serve, and what is difficult today. Your starting point might be unclear positioning, a confusing enquiry journey, or a publishing system nobody wants to use.

Give each agency the same short brief. Include required pages, important integrations, existing brand assets, your preferred launch window, and who will approve the work. You do not need a technical specification to begin, but you do need enough shared context to compare proposals fairly.

sections.title: Read the work, not just the screenshots
paragraphs: Open portfolio websites on your phone. Try the navigation, read a service page, and follow the contact journey. Ask what the agency actually delivered: strategy, identity, design, development, or a smaller part of the project. Distinguish live client work from concept explorations.

Look for relevant problems rather than an identical industry. A team that can explain why it simplified a complex product may be a better fit than one with a visually similar homepage and little explanation of the decisions behind it.
bullets: Ask which project best matches your challenge and why.
Find out how mobile usability, accessibility, and performance are checked.
Request an explanation of any results, including how they were measured.

sections.title: Compare what is included
paragraphs: A lower headline price may exclude content, migrations, revisions, or post-launch support. Ask for a breakdown that makes responsibilities visible. Agree whether the quote covers a fixed number of page templates, individual pages, or a reusable system with content entry.

Make ownership explicit. Confirm who controls the domain, hosting, source files, analytics accounts, and publishing access. Ask how you would move the site or work with another developer later. A good handover should make your business more independent.

rows: Who reviews each stage and how changes are handled
Who writes, supplies, approves, and enters it
Devices, browsers, forms, and accessibility checks
Accounts, documentation, training, and support boundaries

sections.title: Choose a working relationship you can trust
paragraphs: Notice how the team responds to uncertainty. Useful questions and clear trade-offs are more valuable than immediate agreement with every idea. Ask who you will speak to, how progress is shared, and what happens if requirements change.

At ALYOXA, our stated approach connects discovery, strategy, design, development, and launch. Use that sequence as a conversation starter: what will each stage resolve for your particular project? Choose the partner whose reasoning you understand, not simply the most elaborate presentation.

questions.question: Should I choose a local web design agency?
questions.answer: Location can matter for workshops and working hours, but it is only one factor. For a remote partnership, agree communication channels, time-zone overlap, feedback responsibilities, and account ownership before starting.

questions.question: How many agencies should I compare?
questions.answer: A small, relevant shortlist is usually easier to assess than many unrelated proposals. Give each team the same brief and compare scope, reasoning, and responsibilities rather than price alone.

title: Custom website vs template: which is right for your business?
seoTitle: Custom Website vs Template: How to Choose | ALYOXA
description: Compare custom website design and templates across budget, flexibility, content, maintenance, and ownership to choose the right approach for your business.
excerpt: The right foundation depends on your content, your constraints, and what makes the experience distinctive.
intro: Choose a template when an established structure meets your needs and speed or budget is the main constraint. Choose custom website design when your content, user journeys, or brand expression need a system built around them. Neither approach guarantees a better website on its own.
takeaway: Compare complete solutions, including content, setup, maintenance, and future changes. A template price and a finished custom website quote describe different things.

sections.title: Separate design choices from technology choices
paragraphs: A template supplies an existing visual structure. A custom design starts from your requirements. Either can sit on a content management system, and a website builder can support a substantial amount of bespoke design. Custom does not automatically mean hand-editing every page in code.

Ask two separate questions: how will the experience be designed, and how will the finished site be managed? That distinction prevents a false choice between an expressive website and an editing workflow your team can actually use.

sections.title: When a template is a sensible choice
paragraphs: A template can work well for a straightforward business with a stable set of services, a modest content library, and a familiar enquiry journey. It can also help test an early idea before investing in a larger identity or product experience.

Evaluate it using your actual content. Replace the beautiful demo headline with your real headline. Add the length of your service descriptions and the number of items you need to show. If the layout still feels clear on mobile, the structure may be a good fit. If it needs extensive workarounds, the initial saving may become less meaningful.
bullets: Check whether required features need paid extensions.
Confirm that you can edit metadata, navigation, and important content.
Test keyboard navigation and mobile layouts before committing.

sections.title: When custom design earns its place
paragraphs: Custom website development becomes more valuable when several needs interact: an unusual content hierarchy, a distinctive brand story, multiple audiences, or integrations that must fit a specific workflow. The design can organise those requirements together instead of treating each one as an exception.

For example, a business serving both buyers and partners may need two clear paths from the same homepage. That is an illustrative design problem, not a claim about a client result. The value of custom work lies in solving the problem well, rather than adding visual effects for their own sake.

rows: Usually less if the fit is good
Discovery and design are part of the work
Depends on the template and platform
Depends on the agreed system and scope

sections.title: Choose for the next chapter, too
paragraphs: List the changes you reasonably expect: new services, case studies, languages, team members, or a larger resource library. Ask how each option handles them and who would do the work. Include subscription fees, support, licences, and content migration in the comparison.

ALYOXA's digital experiences service connects website strategy, design, development, and responsive systems. If a custom direction is appropriate, begin with what it must achieve and how it will be maintained. If a simpler structure meets the need, unnecessary complexity is not a benefit.

questions.question: Is a custom website better for SEO?
questions.answer: Not automatically. Both approaches can support crawlable content, sound metadata, internal links, and good performance. Judge the implementation and content, not the custom or template label.

questions.question: Can a template website become custom later?
questions.answer: Often, but the cost depends on the platform, content structure, licences, and how much needs to change. Check export and migration options before choosing the initial setup.

title: How much does a custom website cost? What shapes the quote
seoTitle: Custom Website Cost: What Shapes Your Quote | ALYOXA
description: Understand what affects custom website cost, from design and content to integrations and ongoing support, and compare agency proposals on an equal basis.
supportingKeywords: how much does a custom website cost
website design cost for small business
excerpt: Page count is only part of the answer. Understand the work behind a useful, comparable proposal.
intro: Custom website cost depends on the work required: discovery, content, unique layouts, functionality, integrations, quality assurance, and handover. A useful quote explains those responsibilities. Without a defined scope, a single price tells you very little about the finished result.
takeaway: This is a guide to comparing scope, not an ALYOXA price list. Request a project-specific proposal before making budget decisions.

sections.title: Start with the problem and the scope
paragraphs: A small website with original content, distinctive art direction, and a complex booking integration may involve more work than a larger site built from a few reusable layouts. Count the kinds of pages and behaviours, not just the URLs.

Write down what the project must deliver and what already exists. A clear brand identity, approved copy, and organised imagery can reduce uncertainty. If those foundations are missing, the proposal needs to account for creating them or explain who will supply them.

sections.title: Understand the main cost drivers
paragraphs: Discovery and design effort increase when the business serves several audiences or needs a new positioning direction. Development effort increases with custom interactions, complex data, account features, or connections to other systems. Content migration adds a different kind of work: auditing, mapping, editing, and checking what moves.
None of those tasks is inherently wasteful. The question is whether it supports a business need. Ask the team to separate essential launch work from improvements that can follow later.

rows: Unique layouts, art direction, and reusable components
Interactions, integrations, CMS setup, and data handling
Existing URLs, content volume, device checks, and forms
Documentation, training, access transfer, and support

sections.title: Make proposals comparable
paragraphs: Send the same brief to each shortlisted partner and ask them to identify assumptions. A proposal based on supplied copy should not be compared directly with one that includes writing and content entry. A fixed scope and an open-ended support arrangement also carry different responsibilities.

Clarify revision rounds, feedback deadlines, payment milestones, third-party fees, and how additional requests are priced. Agree what counts as completion. A website being online is different from the site being tested, editable, documented, and handed over.
bullets: Are content creation and entry included?
Which integrations and licences are included or billed separately?
Who owns accounts, design files, and the delivered code?
What support is included after launch, and what falls outside it?

sections.title: Plan for running the website
paragraphs: Allow for hosting, domain renewals, platform subscriptions, maintenance, and future content work. Some sites need ongoing development; others need a modest publishing routine and periodic checks. Ask which recurring costs are mandatory and which are optional services.

For an international project, specify currency, applicable taxes, invoicing details, and any exchange-rate assumptions in the proposal. Country names alone do not determine a sensible price. Scope, responsibilities, and the working arrangement are more useful comparison points.

sections.title: Get a more useful first estimate
paragraphs: Share your website or idea, the audience, the desired outcome, must-have functionality, and the launch constraints. Include a budget range if you have one, or explain which decisions you need help prioritising. An honest constraint is more useful than a guessed technical specification.

ALYOXA's enquiry form gives you a place to describe the ambition and project direction. Use the first conversation to establish the scope and the questions that a proposal needs to answer, rather than treating an early estimate as a final commitment.

questions.question: Does ALYOXA have a fixed website price?
questions.answer: This article does not publish a fixed price or package. Contact the studio for a proposal based on your requirements and the work included.

questions.question: Why can two website quotes differ so much?
questions.answer: They may include different levels of strategy, design, writing, functionality, testing, and support. Compare the assumptions and deliverables before deciding that they describe the same project.

title: Website redesign checklist: has your business outgrown its site?
seoTitle: Website Redesign Checklist for Businesses | ALYOXA
description: Use this website redesign checklist to assess business fit, content, navigation, mobile usability, SEO migration, and the scope of a successful redesign.
excerpt: Decide what to keep, what to change, and how to protect the value your current website already has.
intro: A website redesign is worth considering when the current site no longer represents your offer, makes important tasks difficult, or prevents your team from maintaining useful content. Start with evidence. An outdated visual style alone does not tell you whether you need a full rebuild or a focused improvement.
takeaway: Before replacing the site, identify what already works: valuable pages, useful content, search traffic, and the journeys visitors complete successfully.

sections.title: Check whether the story still fits
paragraphs: Read the homepage and key service pages as if you knew nothing about the business. Do they explain what you do today, who you help, and why the offer matters? A company can change faster than its website. Old descriptions, irrelevant work, and an outdated structure can create a gap between the business and its digital presence.

List the specific mismatches. Perhaps you now sell a product alongside services, serve a new audience, or need stronger project explanations. Those changes provide a more useful brief than a general request to make the website look modern.

sections.title: Find the friction in real tasks
paragraphs: Choose a few important tasks and try them on a phone: understand a service, compare options, find evidence, and make contact. Check whether navigation labels are clear, text is readable, and forms work. Invite someone unfamiliar with the site to try the same tasks without coaching.

Use analytics and enquiry feedback where available, but avoid treating one number as the whole diagnosis. Fewer enquiries could reflect traffic quality, seasonality, the offer, or a broken form. A redesign should address a supported problem, not become the default explanation for every business challenge.
bullets: Can a new visitor find the relevant service quickly?
Is supporting evidence close to the decision it informs?
Can someone complete the contact journey on a small screen?
Can your team update the content without a workaround?

sections.title: Treat SEO migration as part of the redesign
paragraphs: Inventory existing URLs before changing the structure. Record pages that receive useful traffic or links, and decide which will stay, move, merge, or disappear. Where a page moves, plan a relevant permanent redirect rather than sending every old URL to the homepage.

Preserve valuable content unless there is a clear reason to replace it. Check titles, canonical URLs, sitemap entries, and internal links after the move. Keep staging environments out of the index, then confirm that the production site is indexable at launch. These are implementation checks, not a guarantee that rankings will remain unchanged.

rows: Keep, rewrite, merge, or remove each important page
Existing forms, integrations, and account ownership
Baseline measures and the improvements to evaluate

sections.title: Choose the smallest scope that solves the problem
paragraphs: If the structure is sound and only a service journey is weak, a targeted improvement may be enough. If the content model, publishing workflow, and technical foundation all constrain the business, a broader redesign may be appropriate. Ask for the reasoning behind a rebuild recommendation.

ALYOXA's approach starts with discovery and strategy before design and development. A redesign brief should similarly connect each proposed change to a real need, then include a migration plan, quality checks, and a clear handover. The launch is a transition to a better working site, not the end of responsibility.

questions.question: How often should a business redesign its website?
questions.answer: There is no universal schedule. Review it when the business, audience, content needs, or technical constraints change. Regular smaller improvements can be more appropriate than rebuilding on a fixed calendar.

questions.question: Will a redesign improve search rankings?
questions.answer: It can improve content and technical foundations, but a redesign does not guarantee rankings. Poor migration decisions can also lose useful URLs and links, so plan redirects and launch checks carefully.

sources.label: Google: site moves with URL changes

title: How to write a website design brief that gets a useful response
seoTitle: Website Design Brief: Practical Template & Guide | ALYOXA
description: Write a clear website design brief with a practical template covering goals, audience, content, functionality, budget, responsibilities, and launch needs.
excerpt: You do not need every answer. You need enough shared context to ask the right questions.
intro: A website design brief explains the business problem, the audience, the desired outcome, and the practical limits of a project. It should help a studio ask better questions and define the work. It does not need to prescribe every screen or technical choice before discovery begins.
takeaway: Be specific about what you know and explicit about what you need help deciding. Uncertainty is useful information when it is visible.

sections.title: Explain why the project exists
paragraphs: Start with a short description of the business and what has prompted the work. A new service, a confusing enquiry process, or a change in audience is more useful context than wanting something premium. Explain what the current website makes difficult and which parts should be preserved.

Define a primary outcome in terms you can evaluate. For example, you might want potential partners to understand your offering and submit an appropriate enquiry. That is a planning example, not a promised result. Avoid making every possible action equally important.

sections.title: Describe the audience and their questions
paragraphs: Tell the studio who will use the website and what they need to know before taking action. Separate primary customers from secondary audiences such as candidates or press. Include real questions from sales conversations if you have them, rather than inventing a detailed persona without evidence.

Share relevant alternatives and references. For each reference, explain what is useful: the clarity of the service structure, the editorial style, or the way a complex process is explained. A collection of links without notes can send the design in several incompatible directions.

sections.title: A website design brief template you can copy
paragraphs: Use these prompts as a working document. A short, honest answer is better than filling every box with general language. Mark assumptions and let the discovery process resolve them.

rows: What you offer, who you serve, and why the site needs to change
What a successful visitor journey should lead to
What people need to understand or trust
Known pages, available copy, imagery, and missing assets
Forms, publishing, booking, accounts, or integrations
Budget guidance, launch dependencies, and required approvals
Decision-maker, content owner, and future site editor

sections.title: Make constraints and responsibilities clear
paragraphs: If there is a deadline, explain what creates it. A fixed event date and an internal preference require different planning. If the budget is not decided, say so and identify which scope decisions you need to compare. Avoid asking for a fixed estimate while leaving major features undefined.

Identify who supplies content and who approves it. Note access requirements for the domain, hosting, existing CMS, and third-party tools. Account ownership can be resolved early without sharing passwords in a public brief; use an appropriate private access process when the work begins.

sections.title: Use the brief to begin a conversation
paragraphs: Review the brief with the studio and invite questions. The useful outcome is a shared understanding of scope, assumptions, risks, and next decisions. A brief should make those visible rather than become a rigid document that prevents a better solution.

ALYOXA's contact journey asks about your direction, idea, and the people behind it. You can start there even if you do not have a finished brief. Keep this template nearby when preparing the fuller project conversation.

questions.question: How long should a website brief be?
questions.answer: Long enough to explain the context, goals, requirements, and constraints clearly. A concise document with specific answers is more useful than a long document that repeats general ambitions.

questions.question: Do I need to choose a CMS before contacting a studio?
questions.answer: Only if it is a genuine requirement. Otherwise describe how your team needs to publish and maintain content, and ask the studio to explain the options and trade-offs.

title: Brand identity vs logo: what does your business actually need?
seoTitle: Brand Identity vs Logo Design: The Difference | ALYOXA
description: Understand the difference between a logo, visual identity, and brand strategy, and decide what your business needs before commissioning design work.
excerpt: A mark introduces you. A connected identity helps every part of the business speak the same language.
intro: A logo is an identifying mark. A visual identity is the system around it, including typography, colour, imagery, and layout. Brand strategy defines the position and ideas that guide that system. The right scope depends on whether your challenge is recognition, consistency, or a more fundamental lack of direction.
takeaway: Do not ask a new logo to solve an unclear offer. First identify what customers need to understand and what makes your business different.

sections.title: Understand the different layers
paragraphs: A logo helps people recognise a business across touchpoints. It may be a wordmark, a symbol, or a combination. It cannot carry every message or explain the entire service by itself. Its effectiveness depends partly on how consistently and appropriately it is used.

Visual identity gives that mark a wider language: type choices, colours, spacing, image direction, and repeatable compositions. Brand identity is often used more broadly to include verbal expression and the ideas a business wants to communicate. Because terminology varies between studios, ask what the proposed deliverables actually include.

rows: Who are we for, and what position should we take?
How do we explain the offer and sound like ourselves?
How do the parts look and work together?
What identifying mark represents the business?

sections.title: Identify the problem before the deliverables
paragraphs: If your positioning is clear and your materials work consistently, a limited logo refinement may be appropriate. If the website, proposals, and social content all look unrelated, a wider identity system may solve a more useful problem. If the offer is difficult to explain, begin with strategy and messaging.

Review a few real touchpoints side by side. Ask whether they feel like the same business, whether information is easy to understand, and whether the identity fits the audience. Personal taste matters, but it should not be the only basis for a business design decision.

sections.title: Ask for a system your team can use
paragraphs: A useful brand identity package includes more than a presentation of ideal applications. It explains everyday use. Your team needs appropriate files, clear guidance, and examples that match the work they actually produce. An elaborate system that nobody can maintain may create more inconsistency.

Agree where the identity must work: small mobile headers, proposal covers, product interfaces, printed materials, or another specific setting. Confirm font and image licensing, export formats, and which templates are included. Those details affect whether the identity is practical after handover.
bullets: Logo variants suited to the intended backgrounds and sizes.
Typography and colour guidance with readable combinations.
Image and layout principles, supported by relevant examples.
Clear ownership, licence information, and accessible working files.

sections.title: Connect the identity to the digital experience
paragraphs: A website is where brand expression meets content and interaction. The design has to remain recognisable while helping people navigate, read, and act. Copy, interface states, photography, and motion all contribute to that experience. Applying a logo and colour palette at the end is rarely enough to connect them.

ALYOXA describes brand systems through positioning, visual identity, art direction, and guidelines. If you are planning both an identity and a website, discuss the relationship early so decisions about the brand can inform the structure and behaviour of the site.

questions.question: Can I start with a logo and add an identity later?
questions.answer: Yes, especially when the immediate need is narrow. Make sure the original design files and usage rights are clear, and expect that a broader positioning exercise may later require changes to the mark.

questions.question: Does a rebrand always require a new logo?
questions.answer: No. A business may need clearer messaging, a better visual system, or improved applications while retaining a recognisable mark. Define the problem before deciding what must change.

title: Website conversion design: help the right visitors take the next step
seoTitle: Website Conversion Design: From Visits to Enquiries | ALYOXA
description: Improve the enquiry journey with clear website messaging, relevant proof, useful calls to action, accessible forms, and a practical measurement plan.
excerpt: A useful next step starts with a clear offer, credible evidence, and less uncertainty along the way.
intro: A website supports enquiries when visitors understand the offer, see relevant evidence, and can complete a clear next step. Conversion design connects those moments. It cannot compensate for an unsuitable offer or irrelevant traffic, and no button treatment guarantees a better conversion rate.
takeaway: Optimise for appropriate enquiries, not clicks alone. Define what a useful conversion means for your business before changing the interface.

sections.title: Define the action that matters
paragraphs: A conversion is an action you choose to measure: a completed enquiry, a booking, or another meaningful step. For a service business, the quality of the enquiry can matter more than the number of submissions. A form that attracts many unsuitable requests may not be helping the sales process.

Agree on the action and how it will be recorded. Keep the distinction between clicking a button and completing the task. If you calculate a conversion rate, use a consistent definition of conversions and visitors or sessions, and document the measurement period. Avoid comparing unlike businesses as if one benchmark fits them all.

sections.title: Answer the next question in the journey
paragraphs: A visitor may need to understand who the service is for, what it includes, whether the team can deliver it, and what happens after contacting you. Organise the page around those decisions. A striking introduction can create interest, but the supporting information needs to earn the next step.

Place relevant proof near the claim it supports. A project explanation can demonstrate how a problem was approached. A genuine testimonial can add a client's perspective. Do not substitute an unsupported statistic or a concept project for verified evidence of a client outcome.
bullets: Explain the service in language a potential buyer would use.
Link to relevant work rather than an unrelated gallery.
Describe the next step and what information is needed.
Keep important details available on mobile, too.

sections.title: Make calls to action and forms understandable
paragraphs: A call to action should say what it does. Labels such as Discuss your project or View the case study give a clearer expectation than a vague instruction. Visual emphasis should help people recognise the main path without making other useful information disappear.

Ask for information that helps the next conversation. Mark optional fields, provide persistent labels, and show specific errors near the relevant input. If you use a multi-step form, preserve answers when people go back or encounter a failed submission. A successful interface also needs a credible confirmation state, not just an animated button.

sections.title: Improve one hypothesis at a time
paragraphs: Write a specific hypothesis before changing the page: visitors may not understand the offer, the form may be asking for information too early, or the contact link may be difficult to find. Choose evidence that would support or challenge that explanation. Use customer conversations and task testing alongside analytics.

Evaluate enquiry quality after a change, and account for shifts in traffic source or campaign activity. With limited traffic, avoid treating a small difference as a proven result. Keep a record of what changed and why so the next decision has context.

ALYOXA connects brand, digital experience, and product design. For an enquiry journey, those disciplines work together when the promise is clear, the interaction is usable, and the next step feels appropriate to the visitor's decision.

questions.question: What is a good website conversion rate?
questions.answer: It depends on the action, audience, traffic source, and measurement method. Establish a reliable baseline for your own business and judge enquiry quality as well as the percentage.

questions.question: Are shorter contact forms always better?
questions.answer: No. A shorter form can reduce effort, but a few relevant questions may improve routing and project fit. Ask only what is useful now, explain requirements, and test the full journey.

title: Website animation: balance expression, accessibility, and speed
seoTitle: Website Animation and Performance: A Practical Guide | ALYOXA
description: Plan website animation that supports the experience: purposeful motion, reduced-motion alternatives, mobile testing, and performance checks beyond a score.
excerpt: Motion should help people feel the idea without delaying their ability to use the website.
intro: Good website animation has a job: explain a relationship, guide attention, acknowledge an action, or express the brand. It also needs to respect loading time, input responsiveness, and motion preferences. A memorable experience should remain understandable and usable when effects are reduced or unavailable.
takeaway: Separate essential information from decorative motion. People should be able to read, navigate, and act without waiting for an effect to finish.

sections.title: Give each animation a reason to exist
paragraphs: An opening sequence can establish a visual language. A card transition can explain where expanded content came from. A hover response can confirm that an element is interactive. These are different roles, and each needs a different duration and level of emphasis.

Audit the page by asking what would become less clear if an effect were removed. Some motion will be mainly expressive, which can still be appropriate, but it should not block an urgent task. Avoid making every heading, paragraph, and control compete for attention at the same time.

sections.title: Budget for loading and main-thread work
paragraphs: A page can download quickly and still feel slow if JavaScript monopolises the browser while the visitor tries to interact. The initial experience includes rendering, hydration, animation setup, and any work triggered by measuring the layout. Evaluate the full sequence rather than the file size of one animation library.

Keep layout reads and writes organised, avoid unnecessary measurements on every scroll event, and initialise distant interactions when they are needed. Transforms and opacity can often reduce rendering work compared with repeatedly changing layout properties, but they are not automatically free. Large surfaces and many simultaneous effects still need measurement.

rows: Can visitors reach the content and navigation promptly?
Are layout measurements or updates repeated unnecessarily?
Does clicking or typing remain responsive during motion?
Does the composition still work without hover?

sections.title: Design the reduced-motion version deliberately
paragraphs: Respect the browser's reduced-motion preference and decide what the alternative should communicate. Removing a large zoom or parallax effect may be appropriate while keeping a simple state change. Do not leave elements invisible because their entrance animation was disabled.

Content and links should exist in the rendered document, and keyboard focus should reveal controls that might otherwise be waiting for a scroll animation. Dialogs need predictable closing and focus return. Touch users need an alternative to information that is only exposed on hover.

sections.title: Measure the real experience, not only the showcase
paragraphs: Test a cold first visit and a return visit separately. Use smaller screens, slower device conditions, keyboard navigation, and reduced motion. Lab tools can identify problems, while field data shows how actual visitors experience the site. One local score is not proof of real-world performance.

Google's recommended Core Web Vitals thresholds are LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP below 200 milliseconds, and CLS below 0.1. These measure different aspects of the experience. A stable layout does not make a blocked interface responsive, and a fast decorative preloader does not necessarily mean the useful content arrived quickly.

ALYOXA's creative technology work includes motion and interactive systems. The useful question is not how much animation a project can contain, but which interactions express the idea while protecting the visitor's ability to use it.

questions.question: Are GSAP animations bad for SEO?
questions.answer: The library name does not determine SEO quality. Important content must be crawlable, and the implementation should remain accessible and responsive. Measure what the effects actually cost on the intended devices.

questions.question: Should a website always use a preloader?
questions.answer: No. An intro can support a particular brand experience, but it adds a waiting experience that needs justification. Consider first-visit duration, repeat visits, skip behaviour, deep links, and reduced motion.

sources.label: Google: Core Web Vitals and search

title: The website design and development process, explained
seoTitle: Website Design & Development Process | ALYOXA Insights
description: Understand the website design and development process, from discovery and strategy through design, build, testing, launch, and a practical handover.
excerpt: A clear process turns a promising idea into a sequence of decisions you can understand and review.
intro: A website project typically moves through discovery, planning, content and design, development, testing, and launch. The stages can overlap, but each should resolve a clear set of decisions. Knowing what happens at each point makes feedback more useful and responsibilities easier to manage.
takeaway: Judge a process by the uncertainty it resolves, not the number of stages in a presentation. Agree deliverables and approval points for your own project.

sections.title: Discovery: establish what the website must do
paragraphs: Discovery brings the business context, audience needs, existing content, and constraints into one conversation. Review the current site if there is one. Identify the primary visitor journeys, important questions, and any integrations or migration requirements. Record open decisions rather than hiding them behind assumptions.

Planning turns that context into a working structure. A sitemap describes the main pages; content requirements explain what each page needs to communicate. Scope and responsibilities should be clear enough that everyone understands what will be designed, built, supplied, and reviewed.

sections.title: Design: connect the story and the interface
paragraphs: Design begins with how information is organised, not just how the first screen looks. Content and layout inform each other. A compelling headline cannot rescue a page that does not explain the service, and a clear outline needs visual hierarchy to become easy to read.

Review key layouts at realistic content lengths and mobile sizes. Agree reusable components, image direction, typography, and interaction principles. Give feedback against the brief: what feels unclear, what does not fit the audience, and what is missing? Consolidated feedback from the agreed decision-maker is easier to act on than conflicting comments arriving separately.

sections.title: Development: make the system work
paragraphs: Development turns the agreed direction into functioning pages, components, content structures, and interactions. The editor's experience matters alongside the visitor's experience. Confirm which content the team can update, how new pages are created, and which changes require development.

Testing should cover more than a large desktop screen. Check navigation, forms, error states, mobile layouts, keyboard access, loading behaviour, and agreed integrations. A test environment should support realistic review without being mistaken by search engines for the production site.

rows: Shared goals, constraints, and open questions
Recorded checks, resolved issues, and launch readiness

sections.title: Launch: verify the live environment
paragraphs: Moving from a preview to a public domain changes the environment. Check domain routing, HTTPS, forms, canonical URLs, redirects, indexing controls, and essential assets on the live site. A successful build is necessary, but it does not prove that every production setting is correct.

Handover should make ownership and next steps clear. Record account access, renewal responsibilities, content instructions, and the process for reporting a problem. Agree which issues are covered by the delivery arrangement and which future changes need a new scope.

ALYOXA presents its approach as discovery and insights, strategy and planning, design and development, then launch and growth. Use those stages to understand the collaboration, while confirming the specific deliverables and review points in the project agreement.

questions.question: How long does a website project take?
questions.answer: Timing depends on scope, content readiness, integrations, and review availability. Ask for a schedule based on those dependencies rather than assuming a fixed duration applies to every website.

questions.question: Can design and development overlap?
questions.answer: Yes, where the direction and dependencies are clear. Establish what is approved, what remains exploratory, and how changes will affect completed work before overlapping stages.

title: Website launch checklist: what to verify before going live
seoTitle: Website Launch Checklist: SEO, Forms & Handover | ALYOXA
description: A practical website launch checklist covering content, mobile usability, accessibility, forms, redirects, indexing, performance, ownership, and live checks.
excerpt: A launch is more than a publish button. Check the details that turn a preview into a working website.
intro: Before launching a website, verify the content, important user journeys, mobile layouts, forms, search settings, redirects, and account ownership. Repeat critical checks on the live domain after publishing. Preview success does not guarantee that production environment variables, routing, or email delivery are configured correctly.
takeaway: Assign an owner to each launch check and keep a rollback plan. A checklist is useful when someone records what was actually tested.

sections.title: Review the content and the main journeys
paragraphs: Read every public page using the final content, not placeholder text. Confirm service descriptions, contact details, project labels, and any claims. Check that images are appropriate and licensed for the intended use. Replace dummy project information rather than letting it appear as real client evidence.

Follow the important paths from entry to completion. Open a service, inspect related work, and find the contact route. Review menus, footer links, legal links, and any downloadable resources. Check that new pages are linked from somewhere useful rather than existing only in a sitemap.
bullets: One clear primary heading and a readable content structure.
Descriptive links and meaningful image alternatives where needed.
Working navigation at small screen sizes and larger text settings.
Clear labels for concepts, examples, and actual client work.

sections.title: Test forms, errors, and keyboard access
paragraphs: Test required fields, invalid input, successful submission, and failure recovery. Verify that a submitted enquiry reaches the intended destination using an approved controlled test. Do not assume that a success animation proves email delivery. Keep server credentials private and check that the correct production environment can access them.

Navigate using the keyboard. Confirm visible focus, sensible control names, and predictable dialog behaviour. Test reduced motion and make sure important content stays visible. A review on your own laptop is not a substitute for checking the actual devices and browsers the project is intended to support.

sections.title: Check search access and URL changes
paragraphs: Give public pages appropriate titles, descriptions, and canonical URLs. Verify that production pages are not accidentally marked noindex and that the sitemap includes the intended canonical pages. Keep private previews and test environments out of search results.

For a replacement site, test the redirect map using old URLs. Missing pages should return an appropriate HTTP 404 rather than a successful response with an error message. A sitemap helps discovery, but it does not guarantee indexing or rankings. After ownership verification, use Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools to inspect important URLs.

rows: Correct content, functional journeys, and intentional noindex
HTTPS, domain routing, indexability, canonical URLs, and forms
Relevant permanent redirects and updated internal links
Valid sitemap and verified search-engine ownership

sections.title: Measure, document, and check again after launch
paragraphs: Run performance checks against the published domain and distinguish lab measurements from real-user data. Inspect loading, interaction, and layout stability separately. A large visual introduction or an image-heavy page needs an honest assessment of what visitors can do while it loads.

Confirm who controls the domain, hosting, code, CMS, and third-party services. Record renewals, backups or recovery arrangements, and the process for future changes. Know how to return to the previous working deployment if a serious issue appears.

At ALYOXA, launch and growth form part of the stated approach. For your project, agree what post-launch verification and support include. Publishing is an important milestone; a working handover is what makes the website usable for the business that owns it.

questions.question: Should I submit a new website to Google?
questions.answer: Verify the domain in Search Console and submit the canonical sitemap. You can inspect important URLs after launch. Discovery and indexing still depend on Google's systems and are not guaranteed by submission.

questions.question: Do I need to test again after deployment?
questions.answer: Yes. Domain settings, redirects, caching, environment variables, and email configuration can differ from a preview. Repeat the critical checks against the live domain.
